participation.text: Citizen men held formal political participation; women’s public work and differing statuses complicate any claim of universal equality.

production.text: Water provision linked household labor to public infrastructure.

coordination.text: Water provision and commercial work connected households with shared places, while civic procedures assigned political powers to a narrower group.

name: Athens: who worked in public?
geographicPrecision: Agora/city locator; no map of citizen residence or political rights.

interval.label: Sixth–fourth centuries BCE
interval.note: Analytical window joining an Archaic vase to Classical evidence. These phases are distinguished in the text; not a single unchanging social system.

question: Can an excluded political voice still be present in a city’s public life?
summary: Athenian public life combined decision-making, religious activity, markets and the work of supplying households. Those activities did not give everyone the same political powers. A water jar, excavated places, a constitutional account and later legal research illuminate different parts of that history. Together they make it possible to study participation and exclusion without erasing the people whose work kept the city functioning.

sections.title: Start with the jar and its own date
sections.text: The Met hydria dates to about 510–500 BCE. Its front shows women with vessels at a fountain; combat appears on the shoulder. Two horizontal side handles helped lift a hydria, and a vertical back handle served dipping and pouring. The shape and painted work give concrete things to inspect. The scene is an artistic representation near the conventional transition to democracy, not a photograph of a fourth-century household or a label identifying each depicted person’s legal status.

citations.locator: Date, description and visible front image

sections.title: Water connected households with public space
sections.text: Fetching water meant obtaining a necessary household resource outside the house. Rotroff and Lamberton compare images with literary accounts and discuss free and enslaved women carrying water, shopping and selling goods. Wealth and status affected who performed burdensome tasks and whose household could assign them to someone else. This evidence complicates elite male prescriptions about keeping respectable women at home. A fountain or market could be publicly used while access, work and power remained unequal.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 7–11, fountain house and public space

sections.title: Formal participation required eligibility
sections.text: The late-fourth-century Constitution of the Athenians describes male enrollment in local civic communities, or demes, at eighteen, with scrutiny of age, free status and parentage. Its account of the Council and Assembly explains procedures by which eligible citizens governed. Women, resident foreigners and enslaved people did not acquire those political powers simply by living or working in the city. Civic descent, religious roles, property and the franchise are distinct questions; exclusion from the Assembly is not evidence that a person had no public presence.

sections.title: Institutions occupied a changing city
sections.text: The Agora held commercial, religious and administrative activities; the Pnyx was a meeting place for the Assembly. Their different functions help distinguish being in public space from holding formal decision-making power. Neither the jar nor one constitutional description covers the whole sixth-to-fourth-century window. The parentage law and its later reestablishment belong to particular phases. A useful comparison follows how rules, institutions and everyday tasks intersected over time, rather than treating Athens as an unchanging community of equal participants.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 348–349, 451/0 and 403 BCE; c330 account

claims.text: Restriction of formal political participation did not mean that women were absent from public work.

deeperReading.title: Do not transfer another vessel’s inscriptions
deeperReading.text: The Agora book illustrates a hydria of about 530 BCE in Würzburg, while the selected Met object is dated about 510–500. The authors discuss painted names, clothing and possible identification of the earlier scene with the Southeast Fountain House. Those details belong to their illustrated vessel and argument. They are not translations or a secure building identification for the Met jar. The map locates the excavated fountain building as a place to investigate water provision, not as proof of where this painted scene took place. Even apparently similar images require object-specific reading.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 6–8, Würzburg 304 and qualified fountain identification

deeperReading.title: Rules did not make every status claim simple
deeperReading.text: Forsdyke uses legal procedures and disputes to examine how enslaved people could seek freedom or claim civic status, often through networks involving citizens. This brings agency and contested boundaries into an account that might otherwise stop at a list of exclusions. Her argument is an interpretation of selective legal evidence, not a count of successful claims or a complete social survey. Court speeches also have interested speakers and audiences. Set their purposes beside the constitutional account’s procedural description and the archaeological evidence of ordinary work; no single source preserves everyone’s experience.

familyActivity.title: Separate work, place and political power
steps: Find the jar’s side handles and the vessels in its painted scene. Describe the task without guessing anyone’s legal status.
On the map, distinguish the Agora, the fountain building and the Pnyx. Which questions concern water, trade or Assembly meetings?
Name one way a person could help a city function without being allowed to vote in its Assembly.
familyActivity.explanation: The jar, constitution and excavated places belong to different dates and types of evidence. Work in public and formal political participation should be investigated together without making them identical.

evidenceReading.title: Whose activity does each record preserve?
evidenceReading.introduction: The passages are source paraphrases. The book’s Würzburg vase and the selected Met vase remain separate objects.

items.label: The selected jar has its own attribution
items.text: The Met dates 06.1021.77 to about 510–500 BCE and identifies women at a fountain house, with combat on the shoulder.
items.interpretation: Describe visible containers and handles. Clothing and a represented task do not by themselves identify the figures as free, enslaved or enfranchised.

items.label: The constitutional account is later
items.text: Part 42 describes male enrollment scrutiny at eighteen; part 43 describes the Council and Assembly.
items.interpretation: Read it in its late-fourth-century context. Do not apply every procedure unchanged to the date of the Archaic vase.

items.label: A social history tests an elite ideal
items.text: The Agora study sets male-authored prescriptions beside evidence of women’s water carrying, commerce and other activity.
items.interpretation: Public work challenges claims of complete seclusion. It does not show that women shared the Assembly’s franchise or that free and enslaved experience was interchangeable.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded C3 explanation with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, distinct reference phases and sourced geographic orientation.
limitations: The Agora book’s introduction, printed map p. 2 and selected pp. 6–11 were consulted, not every chapter. Its illustrated hydria is not the Met vessel.
The Kenyon translation and selected Forsdyke pages were read; no original papyrus audit, complete legal synthesis or population estimate.
More household, gender, resident-foreigner and enslaved-person evidence and independent/human review remain.

placeStudy.title: Athens: public places did different work
placeStudy.description: Approximate place locators separate a mixed civic/commercial square, an excavated fountain building and the Assembly’s meeting place. No exact ancient street, household route or simultaneous building plan is drawn. The pictured fountain is not securely identified with this excavated building.

points.label: Agora — work and civic institutions
points.text: Commercial, religious and administrative activities shared the Agora. Being present here did not itself confer formal political eligibility.

points.label: Southeast Fountain House — water provision
points.text: The Agora book marks the excavated fountain on its end-of-fifth-century plan. Its possible association with an earlier Würzburg vase is qualified; that vase is not the selected Met hydria.

points.label: Pnyx — Assembly setting
points.text: The site account distinguishes meetings on the Pnyx from the Agora’s many uses. Formal participation concerned a restricted citizen group, not every person who supplied or worked in the city.
